content.text: INP measures how long the page takes to show the next frame after a click, tap or key press, not how long your API takes to answer. Its three parts are waiting for a busy main thread, running your handlers and rendering the update. You fix it in the browser, by painting feedback first and yielding real tasks, not by tuning the backend.

The "In stock only" filter on a product listing feels sluggish, and field data puts the page's INP in "needs improvement". The team spends a week caching the products API. Nothing changes, because the filter never touches the network: it filters 20,000 products already in memory and re-renders the list. We rebuilt it and clicked it in headless Chromium 156, unthrottled on a desktop CPU: 240 to 312 ms from click to next frame, across five runs. A version that showed "Updating…" and then waited a full second for an API call measured 16 ms.
The belief: slow interactions come from slow APIs or networks, so INP is something you fix on the backend.

It's an honest mistake. Users do complain that "the button is slow", and many buttons do send a request. The Network panel shows a long bar, the backend is the usual suspect, and a faster API really does make the result arrive sooner. But INP doesn't measure when the result arrives. It measures when the page first reacts, and that is decided on the
INP ends at the next paint

doesn't try to measure every eventual effect of an interaction, such as network fetches and UI updates from other asynchronous operations, but the time the next paint is blocked. It observes clicks, taps and key presses, not hovering or scrolling, and reports the longest interaction on the page, ignoring one outlier for every 50 interactions. Good is 200 ms or less, poor is above 500 ms, at the 75th percentile.
That's why the API version scored 16 ms: the handler set "Updating…" and returned at its first
, and the browser painted that frame right away. The one-second wait happened after the paint, outside INP.
Three parts, all held up by main-thread work
web.dev splits every interaction into three parts:

content.text: Our filter spent 33 to 56 ms in its handler and 203 to 255 ms in presentation delay, rendering roughly 13,000 new list items. And input delay needs no slow handler at all: when a 250 ms task from elsewhere on the page was already running, a click whose handler only changed one line of text measured 216 to 224 ms, nearly all of it input delay.

content.text: In the wrong version, "Updating…" never even appears: it's overwritten before any frame is painted. The right version measured 16 to 24 ms over five runs. The work didn't get cheaper, though: the frame that rendered the filtered list was still a long animation frame of 227 to 347 ms. Yielding moved it after the feedback; it didn't remove it.

blocks.title: A yield isn't a free pass

content.text: Everything after the yield still runs on the main thread. If that continuation is a 300 ms task, the next click that lands during it pays the wait as input delay. For long work, yield between chunks, not just once, and question whether the page needs to render 13,000 rows at all.
How to apply it in your project
Collect INP with attribution from real users, group by
, and pick the worst element on the pages with the most traffic.
Large input delay points at other long tasks on the page; large processing at your handlers; large presentation delay at how much DOM and layout each update causes.
Make the visible change, then yield with
fallback. Move analytics, saving and other invisible work after the yield.
Chunk long loops with a yield between chunks, render only what's visible, and keep reads and writes apart so a handler doesn't force layout.
